For Respondent No. 1 (State): A.W. Bhuiyan, Additional attorney general, (B. Hossain, Assistant Attorney General, with him), instructed by Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on record. 
Respondent No.2: Ex-parte.
parties:
Abdul Hai Khan & ors ------ Appellants 
vs.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This appeal by special leave has arisen from an order of the High Court Division (Jessore Bench) dated 2 February 1986, passed in Criminal Revision No. 20 of 1983 refusing to quash a criminal proceeding which was assailed on the ground that private complaint on which the proceeding started was hit by the mandatory prohibition in Section 195(c), Crl. P.C. The question raised in this appeal relates to the scope and extent of this section.

2. Accused-appellant No.1 had filed Title Suit NoAI0 of 1975 renumbered as Title Suit No.1 of 1979, in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulnaj, against defendant Ashutosh Debnath for specific performance of a contract for sale of a land on the strength of a Bainapatra dated 15 July 1971 executed in his favour by the owner, the said Ashutosh. The suit was, however, dismissed on merit by a judgment dated 15 September 1980 with the observation that the Bainapatra produced by the plaintiff was a forged document. Thereupon, the owner's bargader, Md. Ziad Ali Khan, who is respondent No.2 in this appeal, lodged a complaint on 21 May 1982 before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Khulna, alleging that the Bainapatra had been forged by the plaintiff of the suit who also produced it in court as evidence, and on that complaint cognizance was taken by the Magistrate and process was issued against the plaintiff and four others who had participated in the forgery all of whom are appellants here-under Sections 467, 468 and 471 of the Penal Code. The appellants challenged the proceeding against them by an application under Section 561A, Crl.P.C. taking the ground that the cognizance as taken on a private complaint was totally barred by S.195(1)(c) Crl.P.C. in that when the alleged forged document was produced in evidence in court it was the court alone which was competent to make a complaint. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, however, relying upon a decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Emperor v. Raja Kushal Pal Singh, AIR 1931, All. 443, rejected the contention and refused to quash the proceeding. The learned Judges further observed that since the offence of forgery in respect of the Bainapatra dated 15 July 1971 was committed prior to the institution of the civil suit the suit was filed on 1 June 1975 it could not be said that the offence was committed by a party to the proceeding as contemplated in S.195(1)(c). Leave was granted by us to consider the legality of the order of the High Court Division in view of the fact that judicial opinions are sharply divided on the question involved.

3. Khondkar Mahbub Hossain, learned Advocate has appeared for the appellants and Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney General has appeared for the State, respondent No. 1, to support the decision of the High Court Division. Clause (c) of S.195(1) Cr.P.C. bars the jurisdiction of a criminal court to take cognizance upon a private complaint of certain offences committed by a party to any proceeding in a court in respect of a document when used or produced in that proceeding and empowers only that court before which the proceeding is taken to make a complaint. This section is quoted below: (Relevant portions only):

"195.-(1) No Court shall take cognizance- (a) of any offence punishable under sections 172 to 188 of the Penal Code, except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned, or of some other public servant to whom he is subordinate;

(b) of any offence punishable under any of the following sections of the same Code,namely sections 193, 194, 195, 196, 199, 200, 205, 206, 207, 208, 209, 210, 211 and 228, when such offence is alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any Court, except on the Complaint in writing of such Court or of some other Court to which such Court is subordinate; or (c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 47l, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any Court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, except on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other Court to which such Court is subordinate.

4. As appears, S.195 has put an embargo on the taking of cognizance by Court of certain offences as mentioned therein. Of these offences, those mentioned in clause (a) relate to contempt of lawful authority of public servants; no cognizance of these offences shall be taken except on a complaint in writing of the public servant concerned, or of some other public servant to whom he is subordinate. But to make such a complaint no special procedure has been laid down. However, in respect of the offences described in clauses (b) and (c) which are committed in, or in relation to proceedings in court specified procedure and method for filing complaint by a court have been laid down in S.476, CrI.P.C. Section 476 is quoted below:

"476-(1) When any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court is, whether on application made to it in this behalf or otherwise, of opinion that it is expedient in the interest of justice that an inquiry should be made into any offence referred to in section 195, sub-section (1), clause (b) or clause (c), which appears to have been committed in or in relation to a proceeding in that Court, such Court may, after such preliminary inquiry, if any, as it thinks necessary, record a finding to that effect and make a complaint thereof in writing signed by the presiding officer of the Court, and shall forward the same to a Magistrate of the first class having jurisdiction, and may take sufficient security for the appearance of the accused before such Magistrate or if the alleged offence is non-boilable may, if it thinks necessary so to do, send the accused in custody to such Magistrate,and may bind over any person to appear and give evidence before such Magistrate.

Provided that, where the Court making the complaint is High Court Division, the com- plaint may be signed by such officer of the Court as the Court may appoint.

For the purposes of this sub-section a Metropolitan Magistrate shall be deemed to be a Magistrate of the first class. (2) A Magistrate to whom a complaint is made under sub-section (1) or section 476A or section 476B shall, notwithstanding anything contained Chapter XVI, proceed, as far as may be, to be with the case as if it were instituted on a police report.

(3) Where it is brought to the notice of such Magistrate or of any other Magistrate to whom the case may have been transferred, that an appeal is pending against the decision arrived at in the judicial proceeding out of which the matter has arisen, he may, if he thinks fit, at any stage adjourn the hearing of the case until such appeal is decided."

5. As appears clearly, provisions in S.195, like the provisions is sections 196, 197 and 198 of the CrI. P.C., all appearing in Chapter XV, are exceptions to the general and ordinary powers of a Criminal Court to take cognizance of an offence under S .190 of the said Code. Offences mentioned in clauses (b) and (c) of S.195 relate to proceedings in Civil, Criminal or Revenue Court, and in respect of these offences the legislature has purposely put a restriction on the general jurisdiction of a court to take cognizance that no cognizance shall be taken of any of these offences except on a complaint by the Court concerned. The underlying purposes of this prohibition in clauses (b) and (c) are to prevent a private party from running to the Court with a complaint against their opponents in a proceeding for harassing them or for gratifying their revenge by launching frivolous or baseless prosecution. Again, if the offences described in clauses (b) or (c) are committed in or in relation to a proceeding before a Court, Civil, Criminal or Revenue, it is that court which is in a better position to form an opinion on materials already before it as to whether it is necessary in the interest of justice to make a complaint against the per- sons who are prima facie found to have committed the offences. A private party may be the real victim of the commission of such an offence, but he is debarred from making a complaint directly to the Court; he may, however, initiate the process of filing a complaint by an application under section 476 Crl. P.C., as quoted above, so that the court concerned may hold an enquiry for this purpose.

6. In this case we are concerned with the provision contained only in clause (c) of S.195. It relates to prosecution for certain offences committed in respect of a document produced or given in evidence, such as forgery and use of a forged document in court, by a party to the proceeding. Ingredients of this clause are that an offence, such as the forging of a document, has been committed by a party to a proceeding in any court and that this forged document has been used or produced in that court by a party to the proceeding. If these ingredients are found present in a case, then the mandatory provision against the filing of a private complaint comes into play. In the instant case the appellants have allegedly forged the Bainapatra for purchase of a land and then filed the suit claiming specific performance of the contract as evidenced by the Bainapatra which also they produced in the court in support of their claim. As such these facts should attract the prohibition of clause (c). The learned Additional Attorney General has however argued that though the offence of producing the forged document in court, which is punishable under section 471, was committed by a party to the proceeding, it cannot be said that the offence of forging the document punishable under section 467 was also committed by the appellants as a party to the proceeding, for when the document was forged, in 1971, there was no proceeding in existence; one of them being party to the suit filed subsequent to the commission of the offence will not bring them within the ambit of S.195. By "a party to a proceeding", the learned Addl. Att. Gnlmeans and includes only those persons who were already a party to a proceeding, that is, the offence of forgery has been committed after the institution of the proceeding. He is of opinion that at least the offence under section 467, Penal Code, stands outside the ambit of the prohibition of S.195 and that cognizance of this offence on private complaint is perfectly lawful. The learned Addl. Att. Gnl. has placed reliance upon the Allahabad case, AIR 1931, 443, and strengthened his opinioned referring to a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Patel Laljibhai v. State of Gujrat, AIR 1971 SC 1935 wherein the interpretation of S.195 given by the Allahabad High Court was approved, and it was held that though both the interpretations of S.195 are possible the inperpetration given by the Allahabad High Court was a better one. This decision of the Indian Supreme Court was followed by them in four subsequent cases Ragunath v. State of U.P., AIR 1973, SC 1100; Hohanlal v. State of Rajstan, AIR 1974, SC 299; West Bengal v. Haridas Mundra, AIR 1976, SC 2225 and State of Karnataka vs. Memareddy, AIR 1981, SC 1417.

7. On the other hand, Kh. Mahbub Hossain has referred to a great number of cases in which different High Courts of India and the erstwhile Dacca High Court took the view that when an offence of forgery has been committed in respect of a document which has been used or given in evidence in court, then the case comes within the ambit of provisions in S.195 it being immaterial whether the offence was commit- ted prior, or subsequent to the institution of the proceeding in court. Some of the cases are, Emperor Y. Rajappa, AIR 1936 Born. 221; Basudev R. Joshu, AIR 1923, Born. 105; State of Gujrat v. Ali Bin Razak, 9 Gujrat Law Journal; Harprasad v. Haresram, AIR 1966, All. 124; Vivekananda v. State, AIR 1969, All.189; Hariram v ML Radha, AIR 1943, Nag.327; Subbi Reddy v. Emperor, AIR 1930, Mad. 869; Haribhai v. Bhikubhai, AIR 1965, Guj. 70; Nalini v. Anukul, 21 CWN, 640; In re: Parmesan an, ILR 39, Mad. 677 and Hrishikesh Duttv. State, 20 DLR 66. So far as the Pakistan Supreme Court and the Appellate Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court are concerned, there appears to be no decision on this question. Kh. Mahbub Hossain has placed before us a decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Muslim Khan v. State, 38 DLR(AD) 60, but the question considered there is not exactly on the point now before us. Since the question is of great public importance we propose to examine it at length in order to find the legislative intent in enacting this provision containing the prohibition against taking cognizance on a private complaint.

8. In the case of Raja Kushal Pal Singh, AIR 1931, All. 443, on which the learned Addl. Att. General relied, the offence of forging a document was committed 25 years before the institution of a proceeding in court in which the forged document was given in evidence. The document was no-doubt produced in the court's proceeding by a party thereto but there was no proceeding when they had forged the document 25 years ago. In that connection it was observed:

"An offence which has been committed by a person who does not become a party till, say 30 years after the commission of the offence, cannot be said to have been committed by a party to a proceeding within the meaning of cl.(c). Clause (c), S. 195(1) applies only to cases where an offence is committed by a party as such to a proceeding in any court."

It should be noted that the words "as such" following the word 'party' is not there in the section, but it has been used by the learned Judges to qualify the phrase "party to a proceeding". But as to the other offence, production of the document in court, this offence was of course found by the learned Judges to have been committed by a party to the proceeding in which case a court complaint was necessary.

9. This reasoning of the Allahabad High Court in respect of the offence under section 467 was not supported by the Bombay High Court in the case of Emperor v. Rajappa, AIR 1936 BOM 221 as mentioned above, in which Beaumont Camden the following observations:

"The relevant date which has been considered by the Court is a date the court is invited to take cognizance of the complaint, and all that the court is to see is whether the offence in respect of which it is asked to take cognizance is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any court and in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. It is immaterial that the offence has been committed by the party before the proceedings are taken and the bar contained in s.195(1) (c) will apply if at the time when the court is called upon to take cognizance of a complaint, the accused is a party to a proceeding in a court in which the document has been produced or used as evidence."

The Gujrat High Court in the case of State of Gujrat v. Bhikubhai, AIR 1965 Guj.70, took the view that the legislative intention behind S.195 is to apply the prohibition in respect of a particular class of offenders. It was observed:

"The intention appears to con fume the application of the section only to offenders who happen to be a party to a proceeding. The language used is in general and is intended to include a person who has been a party or is a party to a proceeding. The words party to a proceeding are used in an abstract manner to indicate the only class or category of offenders."

10. The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Patel Laljibhai (AIR 1971 SC 1935) examined the construction of S.195 given by the Allahabad High Court (Raja Kushal Pal Singh's case) and found that the language used in clause (c) of S.195 is capable of two interpretations and accepted the one given by the Allahabad High Court. It was observed:

"The language used seems to us to be capable of either meaning without straining it. We have, therefore, to see which of the two alternative constructions is to be preferred as being more in accord with the legislative intent, keeping in view the statutory scheme and the purpose and object of enacting the prohibition contained in S.195(1)(c) ..... The offence covered by S.471 I.P.C. from its very nature must be committed in the proceeding itself by a party there to..... .It is only with respect to the offences described in S.463 and the offences punishable under section S.475 or S.476, that two views are possible and therefore the effect of reading S.195(l)(c) and S.476 Cr. P.C. together has to be examined for legislative intendment in respect of these offences."

After considering the underlying purposes of the prohibition against private complaint and keeping in view the statutory right of a citizen to make complaint to court under S.190 Cr.P.C., their Lordships concluded as follows:

"It, therefore, appears to us to be more appropriate to adopt the strict construction of confining the prohibition contained in Section 195 (l)(c) only to those cases in which the offences specified therein were committed by a party to the proceeding in their character as such party. The offences about which the court alone is clothed with the right to complain may therefore be appropriately considered to be those offences committed by a party to a proceeding in that court the commission of which has a reasonably close nexus with the proceeding in that court."

<u>11. It appears that the language of clause (c) (1) of S.195 admits of two interpretations-one is that the date of commission of an offence described in S.463 Penal Code is immaterial when the forged document is produced in the proceeding by a party thereto and the other is that the offence under section 463 must be committed after the proceeding is taken. We find it difficult to accept the latter interpretation for a number of reasons. The legislative intent in making the prohibition against a private complaint is to save a party from unnecessary and vexatious prosecution by their opponents and to avoid a conflicting decision between two courts which is quite likely when the criminal court dealing with a private complaint holds that an offence of forgery has been committed by a person who subsequently becomes a party to a proceeding, but the court before which the said proceeding has been taken finds otherwise and holds that no complaint is necessary in the interest of justice. There may be a case in which both the offences, one of forgery of a document before a proceeding is launched and the other its use in a proceeding launched subsequently-have been committed in the course of the same transaction. In such a case both the offences should be tried by the same court in one trial. Difficulty will arise if the prior offence is taken cognizance of on a private complaint and the latter is not brought for trial by a court's complaint. Similar situation will arise if such offences are committed in pursuance of a criminal conspiracy spread over a long period of time. A document may be forged for the purpose of producing it in court to support, say, title to a property. For various reasons a proceeding for enforcement of this claim to title under the forged document may be delayed. If S.195 does not apply in such cases, only because the forgery was committed before institution of the proceeding in which the document was used in court-the purpose of the prohibition will be defeated. To cover both such cases specific provision has been made in sub-section (4) of S.195 itself. It reads thus:</u>

<u>"(4) The provisions of sub-section (I), with reference to the offences named therein, apply also to criminal conspiracies to commit such offences and to the abetment of such offences, and attempts to commit them."</u>

<u>It is therefore, clear that the offences referred to in cl.(c) when committed in pursuance of a conspiracy or in the course of the same transaction, will fall within the ambit of sub-section (4) of S.195 including their abetments or attempts independent of the dates of their commissions.</u>

12. The main ingredient of the prohibitory provision of S.195 is the production in a court proceeding of a forged document by a party thereto. If' a forged document is produced in a proceeding by a party thereto, the court before which the proceeding is pending, will acquire sole jurisdiction to make a complaint if it is of "opinion that it is expedient in the interest of justice". The materials for filing a complaint having already been before it the court is in a better position than a private complainant, to file a complaint not only for the use of the forged document but also for the offence of forging it, irrespective of the date of forgery. On the other hand, if a party to a proceeding has forged a document, during the pendency of the proceeding touching the subject matter of the proceeding, but has not produced it in the proceeding, then the prohibition will not apply and in that case a private complainant is at liberty to file a complaint. Another difficulty may arise if a private complaint is permitted in respect of a document forged prior to the launching of a proceeding. It may be that on conclusion of trial for the forgery it is found that the accused did not forge the document, but used or produced it in the proceeding; he may be acquitted from the charge of forgery but he may be convicted for using it as genuine under section 471 P.C. But this cannot be done because no cognizance of the offence under section 471 shall be taken except upon a complaint by the court concerned. If the interpretation given by the Indian Supreme Court is followed two complaints in respect of virtually the same matter will be required, one by a private complainant and one by the court. This will lead to multiplicity of proceedings which cannot be the Legislative intendment. These two offences, forgery of a document and its production in court, are so interconnected that one cannot be separated from the other when that document has been used or produced by a party to the proceeding in court.

13. The learned Addl. AtGenl. has submitted that when a private complaint is made for an offence under s. 467, the offence thereunder not being committed by a party to a proceeding, the Court also will not be debarred from filing a complaint. We do not think so, for the court has got no inherent power to make a complaint, and the Court will make a complaint only when the commission of an offence falls within the ambit of S.195, and if this section applies, then the court alone, to the exclusion of all other persons, will make the complaint. This view has also been taken by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Bashirul Huq v. West Bengal, AIR 1953 SC 293. In that case the learned Judges also observed that provisions of S.195 cannot be evaded by device or camouflage i.e. by saying that the offences are punishable by some other sections of the Penal Code.

<u>14. Kh. Mahbub Hossain has stressed the words "in or in relation to a proceeding" in any court appearing in S. 476 Crl. P. C. and has argued that the words are wide enough to include an offence committed earlier than the commencement of the proceeding, As I have indicated above, S.476 is not independent of S.195 but it simply lays down the procedure for the court to follow in making a complaint in respect of offences described in S.195. It provides that any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court is to form an opinion whether it is expedient in the interest of justice to hold a preliminary enquiry for the purpose of making a complaint for the offences mentioned in clause (b) and (c) of S.195 allegedly committed in or in relation to a proceeding in that court. This enquiry may be held by the Court either on any application made to it or otherwise, that is, suo-motu. The words 'in or in relation to a proceeding in court have occurred in clause (b) and not in clause (c) of S.195. Nevertheless, these words have been used in S.476 which has laid down a common procedure for both Cl.(b) and Cl.(c). What we find is that the provision in S.476 does not affect, abridge or extend the scope of S.195(b) or (c). The offences mentioned in clause (b) are offences against public justice, such as fabricating false evidence, whether or not committed by a party to a proceeding or whether committed in the proceeding or outside it, but committed in or in relation to a proceeding. But offences referred to in clause (c) must be committed by a party to a proceeding and in respect of a document' produced in court. Scope of each of the two clauses has been clearly expressed in S.195.</u>

<u>15. Here we are concerned with only clause (c) of S.195 CrI. P.C. If the language of a statute is plain and clear admitting of only one construction, then the rule of literal construction shall be adopted whatever may be the consequence. But if the language of the statute is capable of two or more constriations or if the literal construction results in contradiction or leads to absurdity, which could not have been the intention of the Legislature, then the rule of literal construction may be departed from and language of the statute may be modified, if necessary, by addition or alteration of some words. In the case of clause (c) of S.195, it is capable of both the constructions as discussed above and as such it is to be seen which is in accord with the intention of the Legislature. S. 195(1)(c) purposely puts a restriction on the general jurisdiction of a Criminal Court to take cognizance of an offence at the instance of any person under S.190 Crl. P.C. and it empowers a particular court to make complaint for an offence committed by a party to a proceeding in that court in respect of a document produced before it. In the instant case, the Bainapatra appears to have been forged by one of the appellants who thereafter produced it in the proceeding, namely the suit for specific performance of a contract described in it. Both the offences forgery and use of a forged document are closely linked with each other and as such these offences clearly fall very much within the ambit of S.195(c). No cognizance thereof can be taken except on a complaint by the court. It however appears that appellants Nos. 2-5 are not party to the proceeding in question T.S. No. 410 of 1975- in which the allegedly forged document has been produced. As such the bar against cognizance will not apply in their case; but it will apply in the case of Appellant No. 1--who filed the suit and produced the document.</u>

16. For the reasons given above, we allow the appeal in part and direct that the proceedings in respect of Appellant No. 1 only be quashed. This order, however, does not stand in the way of the court concerned in making a complaint according to law.

17. A. T. M. Afzal, J:- I agree with the decision of my learned brother Shahabuddin Ahmed J, but would like to add some of my own reasons in support of the decision.

18. This appeal involves an examination of the scope and applicability of Sec.195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 which reads thus: 195--(1) No court shall take cognizance-

(a) ……………………….

(b) ……………………….

(c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, except on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other Court to which such Court is subordinate. Facts of the case are fully set out in the judgment of my brother. The most important fact to remember, however, is that cognizance of offences under sections 467,468 and 471 has been taken on the basis of a private complaint even though admittedly the document said to have been forged (the Baina Patra, allegedly executed on 15.7.71) was produced and given in evidence by appellant no.1 in T. SAlO of 1975 (re-numbered T.S.1 of 1979) of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna. Quashment of the criminal case was prayed for on the ground that cognizance could not be taken except on a complaint by court as required under section 195(1)(c) Cr. P.C. The High Court Division rejected the prayer relying on a Special Bench Case of the Allahabad High Court, AIR 1931 Allahabad 443, Emperor Vs. Raja Kushal Pal Singh, which laid down that Cl(c) S.195 applies only to cases where an offence is committed by a party, as such, to a proceeding in any Court in respect of a document which has been produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. In other words, the section does not apply where the offence has been committed prior to the offender becoming a party to the proceeding in court.

<u>19. The question precisely before us is whether this restricted interpretation of clause (c) is correct In the impugned judgment it has been observed that the aforesaid Allahabad decision has been followed in a number of cases by our High Court Division. But no such case has been edited in the judgment. Neither the learned Additional Attorney- General nor the learned counsel for the appellants could cite any other case from the High Court Division where this restricted meaning of clause (c) was accepted following the Allahabad decision. I have, however, come across one such case reported in 39 DLR (HCD) 109= 1985 BLD 193 =BCR 1985 HCD 150 (Mst. Saleha Khatun Vs. State). Incidentally, that case and the present case are both from the jessore Bench.</u>

<u>20. As against the aforesaid view the preponderance of judicial opinion has been that the clause applies also to a case where the commission of the offence is anterior to the offender becoming a party to a proceeding in court. Let me call this the wider interpretation of the clause. The High Court of Calcutta, Lahore, Madras, Nagpur, Rangoon and the Judicial Commissioner's courts of Sind have taken this wider view. (vide AIR commentaries: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 3rd (1946) Edition, V.V. Chitaley and K.N. Annaji Rao). According to this view, the proper test to be applied for the purpose of determining the applicability of the clause is to see whether the offender is or has been a party to a proceeding in any court not on the date of the commission of the offence but on the date when the Criminal Court is invited to take cognizance of the offence. To refer to only one case of this line, AIR 1943 Nagpur 327, Vivian Bose J observed "all the High Courts are now agreed that once a forged document is brought into court, then private complaints subsequent to this are barred by S. 195 even in respect of anterior forgeries-s-anterior, that is, to the litigation."</u>

21. To my knowledge this view has been consistently followed in the erstwhile Dhaka High Court. Reference may be made to the case reported in 20 DLR Dhaka 66. I an not aware of any decision nor any has been brought to our notice except the two cases of the Jessore Bench referred to above where the High Court Division has followed the restricted interpretation given by the Allahabad High Court.

<u>22. As for myself I am inclined to favour the view taken by the majority of the High Courts, for, in my opinion upon a plain reading of the language of clause (c) the said view exfacie appeals to reason. The gloss put by the Allahabad decision AIR 1931 Allahabad 443 that the offence must be alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding "as such", I say with respect, amounts to straining the language used by the legislature which is opposed to the ordinary rules of construction. Secondly, the said view is likely to create a chaotic situation in the administration of justice. For example, according to the said view, the criminal proceeding relating to forgery in the present case started on a private complaint can go on as the said offence was allegedly committed in 1971 prior to the offender becoming a party to the Civil suit in 1975 where the document (Baina Patra) was produced in evidence. There will thus be parallel proceedings in the civil court and the criminal court where the same issue, that is, alleged forgery of the document will come to be determined and it is quite likely that the two courts may give contradictory decisions. Then again the offence of using the forged document as genuine (S 471 P.c.) cannot be taken cognizance of by the Criminal court in any case, even according to the Allahabad view, without a complaint by court as the said offence is committed in the nature of things by the offender after becoming a party to the proceeding (civil suit). Thus although the offence of forgery may be tried simultaneously while the proceeding is pending in the Civil Court, the offence of using a forged document must wait until a complaint is made by the civil court. The two offences are so inseparably linked indeed the latter offence is dependent on the former that it cannot be conceived that the trial of one offence may be made dependent upon a possible complaint by the court while the other of-fence is tried upon a private complaint. This will be certainly an anomalous situation which the legislature could not have intended.</u>

23. Perhaps it should have been already mentioned that the Supreme Court of India, however, has approved the Allahabad view as the better view in the case of Patel Laljibhai Sombabhai Vs The State of Gujrat, AIR 1971 Supreme Court 1935. In this case the question has been considered at length, the Allahabad view endorsed and in several subsequent cases it was followed. (vide AIR 1973 S.C.I00, AIR 1974 S.C.299 AIR 1976 SC 2225 and AIR 1981 SC 1417. It is, therefore, fit and proper to consider the reasons given in the case of Patel Laljibhai and to see whether the restricted view of clause (c) is really the better view.

24. It will be seen that at the center of the controversy lies the phraseology 'committed by a party to any proceeding in any court' occurring in clause (c). According to Allahabad view and as approved by the Supreme Court of India, to attract the prohibition contained in CI(c) the offence should be alleged to have been committed by the party to the proceeding in his character as such party, which means after having become a party to the proceeding, whereas according to other High Courts, the prohibition will be applicable even if the offence is alleged to have been committed by the party to the proceeding prior to his becoming a party to the proceeding provided that the document in question is produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. If the aforesaid phrase were not there, there would not be any controversy as to the application of clause (c) irrespective of the fact whether the alleged offence was committed by the party prior to or after becoming a party to the proceeding. It is significant that in India the said phrase has been omitted in the amended code of 1973. Sec. 195(l)(c) now reads as follows: 195 (1) No courtshipsh take cognizance--

(a)……………………..

(b) …………………….

(ii) of any offence described in Section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the said code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in a proceeding in any court, or

iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit, or attempt to commit or the abetment of, any offence specified in sub-clause (i) or sub-clause (ii) except on the complaint in writing of that court or of some plaint other court to which that court is subordinate. From the aforesaid amendment it is reasonable to infer that the legislative intent has always been to make the provision applicable to all cases irrespective of the fact whether the offence alleged was committed prior to or after becoming a party to the proceeding in which the document in question is produced or given in evidence.

25. The Supreme Court of India observed in the aforesaid judgment that the language used in clause (c) is capable of either meaning (two views indicated above) without straining it, "We have, therefore, to see", the judgment says, "which of the two alternative constructions is to be preferred as being more in accord with the legislative intent, keeping in view the statutory scheme and the purpose and object of enacting the prohibition contained in section 195(1) (c)."

26. As regards purpose and object, there cannot be two opinions on what has been stated in the said judgment: The underlying purpose of enacting S. 195 (l)(b) and (c) and S.476 sums to be to control the temptation on the part of the private parties considering themselves aggrieved by the offences mentioned in those sections to start criminal prosecution on frivolous, vexatious or insufficient grounds inspired by a revengeful desire to harass or spite their opponents. These offences have been selected for the court's control because of their direct impact on the judicial process. It is the judicial process, in other wards the administration of public justice, which is the direct and immediate object or victim of those offences and it is only by misleading the courts and thereby perverting the due course of law and justice that the ultimate object of harming the private party is designed to be realized. As the purity of the proceedings of the court is directly sullied by the crime, the court is considered to be the only party ensiled to consider the desirability of complaining against the guilty party.'

27. Since, however, the private party who is ultimately injured is precluded from filing any com- the Supreme Court is of the view that;

"The offences about which the court alone, to the exclusion of the aggrieved private parties, is clothed with the right to complain may, therefore, be appropriately considered to be only those offences committed by a party to a preceding in that Court, the commission of which has a reasonably close nexus with the proceedings in that Court so that it can without embarking upon a completely independent and fresh inquiry, satisfactorily consider by reference principally to its records the expediency of prosecuting the delinquent party. It, therefore, appears to us to be more appropriate to adopt the strict construction of confining the prohibition curtained In Section 195(l)(c) only to those cases in which the offences specified therein were committed by a party to the proceeding in the character as such party."

28. Speaking with great respect, I have found myself unable to agree with the above conclusion having regard to the legislative intent, purpose and object of the enactment so lucidly set out and as quoted above as a prelude to the conclusion.

29. When the direct and immediate object of the offences in question is to subvert the administration of justice and the Court considered to be the only party entitled to consider the desirability of complaining against the guilty party, it is, in my opinion, immaterial whether the offence was committed after becoming a party to the proceeding or without. The guilt remains the same and the Court's authority and responsibility do not become any the less. As regards close nexus between the offence and the proceeding, the same is established as soon as the document is produced or given in evidence; the nexus is not dependent on the time of commission of the offence alone. Rather the introduction of the document in the proceeding, even though the offence might have been committed prior to the proceeding brings about such a co-relation between the two, subversion of public justice being the object of the producer of the document, that the court, as a matter of public policy, is then considered, to the exclusion of the private complainant, to be the only party entitled to consider the desirability of complaining against the guilty party.

30. More often than not the genuineness or otherwise of such a document falls to be determined in the proceeding itself, for example, in the present case Ute Bainapatra was found to be forged. There- fore, although the offence is not committed as a party to the proceeding as such, the court before lodging a complaint does not have to embark upon an in dependent] and fresh inquiry and can satisfy itself from its record as to the expediency of prosecuting the delinquent party. Thus the reasons given for restricting the offences to only those offences committed by a party to a proceeding in that Court in the character as such party" do not seem to be in keeping with the object and purpose of enacting the prohibition against private complaint.

<u>31. In the Allahabad Case as also in that of the Supreme Court of India, the Statutory scheme has been noticed by making reference to Sec.476 Cr.P.C. which prescribes the procedure for making complaint in cases mentioned in Sec. 195(1)(b) and (c). The learned Judges of Allahabad High Court put emphasis on the following words occurring in S.476 .... "which appears to have been committed in or in relation to a proceeding in that Court and held that S.476 and CI(c). S.195 have the same scope meaning that S.476 contemplates commission of the offence in course of the proceeding and not outside it. The proposition in no doubt means the same but the clause in relation to in my opinion, is wide enough to take in offences committed prior to the proceeding. The dictionary meaning of the worn 'relation', inter alia, is way in which on stands or IS related to another, kind of connection or correspondence or contrast or feeling that prevails between persons or things. True, at the time the offence was committed there was no proceeding and as such the offence could not be in relation to any proceeding but the nexus or relation comes into being as soon as the document is produced in the proceeding. I am, therefore, inclined to think that reading Cl.(c) with Sec.476 of the Code, there does not seem to be any compelling reason to restrict the application of the said clause limiting the control of the court only to few offences (committee defendant late) as would be the practical result of such interpretation.</u>

32. The penultimate paragraph in the judgment of the Indian Supreme Court ( AIR 1971 Sc 1935) quoted below, in my opinion, sums up the whole argument in favour of the wider interpretation of clause (c) : "The purpose and object of the Legislature in creating the bar against cognizance of private complaints in regard to the offences mentioned in Section 195(1)(b) and (c) is both to save the accused person from vexatious or baseless prosecutions inspired by feelings of vindictiveness on the part of the private complainants to harass their opponents and also to avoid confusion which is likely to arise on account of conflicts between findings of the Courts in which forged documents are produced or false evidence is led and the conclusions of. the criminal Courts dealing with the private complaint. It is for this reason as suggested earlier, that the Legislature has entrusted the Court, whose proceedings had been the target of the offence of perjury to consider the expediency in the larger public interest of a criminal trial of the guilty party."

<u>33. Finally I take the view that Cl.(c) of Sec. 195 (I) Cr. P.C. does not bear a restricted interpretation. In other words, the clause will be applicable even when the offence alleged is committed by the party to a proceeding in any court before becoming such party provided the document is produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. Thus the view taken by the High Court Division is found to be not correct.</u>
